transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-02-12 10:00 PT / 18:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Aisha (Redwood AE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Lena (Redwood CSM), Jared (Moneta CTO), Priya (ML Eng), Marcus (SRE), Tanya (PM)

Auto-summary (brief):
- Reviewed last week's pilot numbers; caching produced ~28% token cost reduction on chat flows with stable prefixes.
- Batching improved throughput but increased p95; tradeoffs discussed for user-facing vs background workloads.
- Action items assigned to run concurrent benchmarks and share cost model spreadsheet.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Aisha: Hey everyone, thanks for joining the Moneta weekly—happy to be back. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Jared: Jared here.
[00:10] Priya: Priya.
[00:12] Marcus: Marcus.
[00:13] Tanya: Tanya.
[00:15] Carlos: Carlos, Redwood SE.
[00:17] Aisha: Cool. We put the bench slides in the doc earlier, but Carlos will run us through the token/sec and cost per unit numbers first.
[00:25] Carlos: Alright, jumping in. Reminder: baseline run was hosted small model variant, no cache, batch size 1, sequence avg ~370 tokens. Baseline throughput was ~220 tokens/sec for the cluster we used, cost ~ $3.40 per million tokens when you include infra + model price.
[00:48] Priya: Wait, is that with quantization?
[00:50] Carlos: No, baseline was fp16. We then ran two more configs: prefix-only caching with fp16 and a quantized int8 variant with caching. Prefix caching cut duplicate prefix compute so effective tokens processed dropped, giving us about a 28% reduction in billed tokens for the chat flow we tested — mainly because a lot of our prompts had repeated system/preamble tokens.
[01:15] Marcus: When you say billed tokens dropped, are you talking about server-side accounting or client-side dedupe? We need clarity for our finance team.
[01:23] Carlos: Good call — it's server-side reduction: the inference runtime reused KV cache so those tokens weren't recomputed, which we map in the cost model as saved model compute. Billing in hosted mode still shows token ingress but our cost model subtracts cached tokens from per-token compute cost. We'll hand you the spreadsheet that breaks that down.
[01:40] Aisha: The key metric we want you to look at is tokens/sec per dollar — i.e., how many tokens the system can sustainably generate for each dollar of spend, factoring caching and batching.
[01:52] Priya: Do you have a number for tokens/sec/$ after caching?
[01:55] Carlos: Yes — with prefix caching enabled and same batch size, tokens/sec/$ improved from ~65 tokens/sec/$ baseline to ~88 tokens/sec/$, so roughly a 35% uplift. For int8 quantized run plus caching we saw ~112 tokens/sec/$ but p95 moved a bit.
[02:18] Tanya: How bad did p95 get? We can't have UI visible latency degrade.
[02:21] Carlos: For the int8 + batch 8 run p95 jumped from ~180ms to ~420ms in the worst buckets; average stayed ~160-220ms. So background workloads like embeddings/rerank can use larger batch sizes; for interactive chat we recommend batch 1-2 or adaptive batching.
[02:44] Jared: Are these results on your hosted infra or our dedicated pool? We've only got the dedicated pilot nodes running in our staging VPC, and numbers might differ.
[02:52] Carlos: Good point — these were on Redwood hosted cluster that mirrors your dedicated config but not identical. We need to run the high-concurrency pass on your dedicated pool to validate. That's one of our action items.
[03:05] Priya: Also curious about cold-start vs warm requests. Do cached prefixes really help cold calls?
[03:12] Carlos: Caching helps warm sessions dramatically; cold sessions still pay kv init costs. Prefix caching is most impactful when there's a consistent system prompt or repeated preamble. For Moneta's product, looks like ~40% of sessions share a common preamble, so big win.
[03:30] Marcus: Any notes on model fallbacks? If your dedicated pool saturates, will routing to a smaller quantized variant keep latency within SLO?
[03:37] Aisha: Yes we can configure automatic fallback to compatible variants — that's in the rollout policy. But remember quality/regression checks — we'll need to run evals on the smaller variant to ensure acceptable output.
[03:48] Carlos: I want to call out the batching tradeoff more concretely: when we increase batch size from 1 to 8, tokens/sec increases ~2.9x, but p95 for single-token completions often doubles. For long completions the amortized cost per token goes down a lot. So workload shape matters. We recommended two profiles in the pilot: interactive profile (batch 1-2, caching on) and bulk profile (batch 8-16, quantized) for background jobs.
[04:16] Priya: That split sounds reasonable. For rerank, we can go bulk. For chat, keep it low.
[04:21] Tanya: On the cost spreadsheet — does it include network egress and storage for logs/kv? We have compliance retention costs to factor.
[04:27] Aisha: The baseline sheet includes model compute and infra. We'll add a separate line item for egress and audit log storage; we'll also show a couple of scenarios for 30/90/365 day retention.
[04:38] Jared: Can you show how caching savings scale with user concurrency? If caches are per-session and sessions are ephemeral, do we lose the benefit at scale?
[04:46] Carlos: Excellent question — there are a few caching approaches. Per-session prefix cache is highest win but limited to session lifespan. We also can use a shared prefix cache for common prompts which scales better. In our runs, at 200 concurrent sessions with 40% shared preamble, effective saved tokens stayed within 70-80% of single-session savings because of reuse. We'll validate with the dedicated run.
[05:10] Priya: What's the modeled cost per 1M tokens for int8 + cache vs fp16 baseline?
[05:14] Carlos: Quick numbers from the sheet: fp16 baseline roughly $3.40 / 1M tokens. fp16 + prefix cache effective compute cost ~ $2.45 / 1M tokens after amortizing caching. int8 + cache dropped to about $1.90 / 1M tokens in our hosted run assumptions. Link with full calc will be in the spreadsheet.
[05:36] Marcus: Those are promising. But we need to see p95 distributions — not just averages.
[05:41] Carlos: Agree. We'll produce p50/p95/p99 CSVs per run.
[05:45] Aisha: Quick callout on instrumentation — make sure your telemetry tags user intent vs system tokens. We've seen some customers accidentally include large embedded artifacts as system tokens which skews cache effectiveness.
[05:58] Priya: Good note. We'll scrub sample prompts.
[06:02] Carlos: For the high-concurrency test we'll run three toggles: cache off, prefix cache on, prefix+shared cache on; and for each we'll run batch sizes 1, 4, and 8. Expect CSVs with token/sec, p50/p95/p99, and cost estimated.
[06:20] Aisha: Timeline: Carlos runs the tests Friday (2/14), I send cost model 2/14, customer shares prompt sample by 2/18, then we reconvene next Tuesday to review.
[06:30] Tanya: Can we also add a quick security check item — SSO and KMS integration status? We're trying to align compliance gate with pilot completion.
[06:36] Lena: I'll pull the security docs and status — Redwood's SSO/SAML, KMS integration notes and SOC2 artifact checklist. I'll attach to the deck.
[06:44] Jared: Sounds good. One more thing: can you annotate the spreadsheet with assumptions about tokenization differences? We're using a custom tokenizer wrapper which slightly changes token counts.
[06:53] Carlos: We'll add a multiplier column so you can plug in tokenization ratio.
[06:57] Tanya: Great.
[07:00] Aisha: Any other blockers?
[07:02] Priya: None from our side.
[07:04] Marcus: No.
[07:05] Jared: We're good.
[07:06] Aisha: Awesome. Recap: Carlos runs concurrency benchmarks with toggles; Aisha shares cost model; Priya sends prompt sample and SLOs; Lena provides security docs. We'll meet next Tuesday same time. Thanks all.

End of transcript.
